answers.q: What does the DeepGrid portfolio consist of, and how many chips are planned?
answers.text:
DeepGrid Plans Eleven Mature-Node SKUs Plus a Separately Funded Drone SoC
The DeepGrid product portfolio consists of eleven mature-node chips targeting defence, industrial, and energy infrastructure, alongside one separate advanced-node device, bringing the total portfolio to 12 planned chips.
Composition of the Eleven Mature-Node SKUs
The primary mature-node lineup encompasses eleven distinct chips across power, sensing, control, and secure computing: SKU-1 BLDC Motor Controller, SKU-2 Smart-Meter SoC, SKU-3 Hi-Rel PMIC, SKU-4 Lockstep MCU, SKU-5 Interface Transceiver, SKU-6 Voltage Supervisor, SKU-7 4D Radar RF, SKU-8 Display Driver, SKU-9 SDV Zonal Gateway, SKU-10 DG32-Max Secure MCU, and SKU-11 SOH-Aware BMS Controller.
Nine of these mature-node designs are slated for prototyping on the ChipFoundry December 2026 shuttle, while SKU-7 and SKU-11 remain outside this initial shuttle run.
Track B Drone SoC Architecture and Funding Scope
In addition to the eleven mature-node chips, the portfolio includes D100, a Track B 28 nm drone SoC. This device does not have an active shuttle plan line and operates under an independent financial structure.

answers.q: Which chips go on the December 2026 shuttle?
answers.text:
Nine of Eleven Blueprint SKUs Are Slated for the December 2026 Shuttle
DeepGrid's plan schedules nine of its eleven blueprint chips for the ChipFoundry December 2026 prototype shuttle run, excluding only the radar front-end and BMS controller.
Included Prototype Chips
The prototype shuttle scheduled for late December 2026 includes SKU-1 (BLDC Motor Controller), SKU-2 (Smart-Meter SoC), SKU-3 (Hi-Rel PMIC), SKU-4 (Lockstep MCU), SKU-5 (Interface Transceiver), SKU-6 (Voltage Supervisor), SKU-8 (Display Driver), SKU-9 (SDV Zonal Gateway), and SKU-10 (DG32-Max Secure MCU).
The operational deadline for this tape-out is set for 26 December 2026, representing approximately ₹2.6 Cr in prototype runs across SKU-1 through SKU-6 and SKU-8 through SKU-10.
Excluded Designs and Program Scope
Two portfolio chips are omitted from this shuttle slot: SKU-7 (4D Radar RF), whose front end is still in development, and SKU-11 (SOH-Aware BMS Controller), which remains at the specification phase without an assigned multi-project wafer slot.
Additionally, the 28 nm Track B drone SoC (D100) carries no plan line and is not slated for this shuttle run.

answers.q: What process node are the first DeepGrid chips built on?
answers.text:
Initial DeepGrid Chips Target 130 nm and 180 nm Mature Nodes
DeepGrid's initial product line is built on mature process nodes, specifically 130 nm and 180 nm, before migrating to finer geometries in later years.
Initial Deployment Across 130 nm and 180 nm Processes
The company's immediate product rollout focuses on 130 nm and 180 nm processes across multiple initial SKUs. For instance, SKU-1 (BLDC Motor Controller) is designed as a 130 nm chip targeting 100 MHz on SKY130. Similarly, SKU-2 (Smart-Meter SoC) is slated for a 130 nm implementation at 100 MHz on its first multi-project wafer (MPW) run alongside SKU-1, with plans for an SCL 180 nm variant.
Other initial microcontrollers and peripheral parts also use this dual-node baseline. SKU-4 (Lockstep MCU) is scheduled for a December 2026 shuttle as a 130 nm chip at 100 MHz, followed by an embedded-flash variant on SCL 180 nm. Similarly, SKU-3 (Hi-Rel PMIC) deploys a sky130 prototype for digital sequencer logic while targeting SCL 180 nm for the 28 V front end and power stage.
Specialized 130 nm SiGe and Long-Term Node Migration
For high-frequency requirements where standard CMOS is insufficient, DeepGrid utilizes specialized 130 nm Silicon-Germanium (SiGe). Chip 7, a 4D radar front end operating at 77 GHz, uses the IHP SG13G2 130 nm SiGe process because standard 130 nm CMOS cannot reach millimeter-wave frequencies.
Migration beyond mature 130 nm and 180 nm nodes is deferred to future roadmaps. The architecture roadmap plans a transition to 90 nm, 55 nm, and 45 nm beginning in 2028, followed by 28 nm nodes from 2030 onward.

answers.q: How much is DeepGrid raising in the first tranche and what will the money be spent on?
answers.text:
DeepGrid Plans a ₹10 Cr First Tranche to Fund Prototypes, Engineering, and Initial Approvals
DeepGrid plans to raise ₹10 Cr in Tranche 1 to tape out nine prototype chips on a December 2026 shuttle and fund early testing, team expenses, and respin reserves.
Prototype Shuttle Runs and Board Bring-Up
The plan allocates ₹2.6 Cr to produce nine prototypes on the December 2026 shuttle covering SKU-1 through SKU-6 and SKU-8 through SKU-10. Each prototype costs about ₹0.29 Cr, covering a $15,000 slot alongside $15,000 for IP and other expenses. An additional ₹0.1 Cr is designated for bring-up and evaluation boards.
Respin Reserves and Operational Contingency
To mitigate manufacturing risks without stalling operations, ₹2.5 Cr is earmarked as a respin reserve to cover approximately eight prototype re-runs at ₹0.29 Cr each. DeepGrid also sets aside ₹0.3 Cr as a general contingency fund, which handles board respins.
Engineering, Tooling, and First Approvals
The remaining ₹4.5 Cr is dedicated to personnel, tools, and regulatory milestones. Engineering team costs receive ₹2.5 Cr (₹1.0 Cr through March 2027 and ₹1.5 Cr for the subsequent 12 months). Electronic design automation (EDA) licences and lab test equipment account for ₹1.0 Cr, while the final ₹1.0 Cr funds initial approvals, including military screening for SKU-6 and partner meter certification.

answers.q: What is the total funding plan across tranches?
answers.text:
DeepGrid Plans ₹50 Cr Across Two Tranches for Mature Silicon
DeepGrid's mature-node silicon portfolio is planned across two sequential tranches totalling ₹50 Cr, comprising an initial ₹10 Cr raise to tape out nine chips followed by a ₹40 Cr raise to carry them to commercial production.
Allocation across Tranche 1 and Tranche 2
Tranche 1 is a proposed ₹10 Cr round designated to take nine prototype chips to tape-out on a December 2026 shuttle (costing ₹2.6 Cr), alongside a ₹2.5 Cr prototype respin reserve, ₹2.5 Cr for the engineering team, ₹1.0 Cr for first approvals, ₹1.0 Cr for EDA tools and lab equipment, ₹0.3 Cr for general contingency, and ₹0.1 Cr for bring-up boards.
Tranche 2 is planned for May 2027 at ₹40 Cr, scheduled to be raised once prototypes demonstrate working silicon on test boards, to fund full production qualification and commercialization.
Separate Round and Financial Model Variance
Outside of the two mature-node tranches, the company outlines a separate ₹50 Cr round earmarked specifically for Track B (the D100 Drone SoC).
In addition to the Blueprint's ₹50 Cr baseline across two tranches, the company's September financial model outlines raising ₹55 Cr, combining ₹45 Cr in equity with a ₹10 Cr loan backed by CGTMSE.

answers.q: What clock speed has the DG32-LITE lockstep core actually reached after place and route?
answers.text:
DG32-LITE Lockstep Core Achieves 55 to 62 MHz in Post-Route Timing
In post-route static timing analysis on the 130 nm process, the DG32-LITE lockstep core closes at 55 to 62 MHz, which defines the operational 50 MHz clock speed of the pre-silicon chip.
Post-Route Timing Results Across Blocks
Static timing analysis after place-and-route shows the lockstep core reaches a maximum frequency of 55 to 62 MHz on the SkyWater 130 nm process. While hardened peripherals such as GPIO, PWM, and the lockstep checker clear over 90 MHz, the lockstep core acts as the limiting critical path for the entire single-domain die.
Distinction Between Design Targets and Implementation
The 55 to 62 MHz post-route closure directly explains why the preliminary engineering datasheet specifies an operating clock of 50 MHz. Although high-level portfolio documents cite a 100 MHz target for SKU-4, company materials identify 100 MHz as an unachieved design target rather than an implemented post-route frequency.
Physical silicon measurements are not yet available because the DG32-LITE design is currently pre-silicon.

answers.q: What does SKU-2 do and which market is it for?
answers.text:
SKU-2 Energy-Metering SoC Architecture and Target Markets
SKU-2 is an energy-meter SoC designed to combine analog metering front ends, compute logic, billing cryptography, and tamper tracking onto a single 130 nm chip targeting five distinct electricity metering and submetering markets.
On-Chip Functional Architecture
SKU-2 integrates dedicated metrology arithmetic and converters to replace two-chip implementations consisting of a standalone metering analog front end and an external microcontroller. Specifically, a six-channel 24-bit sigma-delta front end feeds a sinc³ decimator and a dedicated hardware metrology engine that calculates active, reactive, and apparent power as well as total harmonic distortion up to the 15th harmonic.
For system execution and data protection, the architecture incorporates a DGridRiscV core, four-channel direct memory access, and a DG-SE hardware security engine running AES-256 and SHA-256 to protect billing information. An always-on power management unit and real-time clock running off a 32.768 kHz crystal draw under 2 µW with brownout detection to preserve system time and tamper status when grid power is lost.
Target Application Markets
The company targets five application areas wherever electricity is billed or measured: household meters; distribution transformer (DT), feeder, and commercial & industrial (C&I) metering; rooftop-solar net metering; electric vehicle (EV) chargers; and building submetering or smart plugs.
Across these five target areas, the portfolio model projects an aggregate addressable market of 16 million to 45 million units annually at unit prices spanning $0.80 to $10.00, representing an estimated annual addressable opportunity of ₹273 Cr to ₹1,794 Cr.

answers.q: What revenue does the plan project for FY2031?
answers.text:
FY2031 Revenue Projected at ₹608 Cr for Chips and ₹594.3 Cr Company-Wide
The SKU Blueprint projects FY31 chip revenue ramp at ₹608 Cr, whereas the September 2026 financial model projects total company revenue of ₹594.3 Cr with only ₹45.0 Cr from semiconductors.
Chip ramp projections and run-rate targets
Under the October 2026 SKU Blueprint, chip revenue is projected to ramp to ₹608 Cr in FY31 based on expected approval timelines, while reaching ₹948 Cr by FY33. The full run-rate capacity of all eleven chips totals ₹1,000 Cr, which serves as a long-term plan line and an FY31 stretch target rather than an expected baseline.
Divergence between planning documents
The SKU Blueprint and the September 2026 financial model reflect fundamentally different baseline assumptions rather than consolidated numbers. While the Blueprint models ₹608 Cr strictly from chip sales, the financial model outlines ₹594.3 Cr across the entire business, driven heavily by its Systems segment (₹501.9 Cr), Robotics (₹28.9 Cr), and Sensors (₹18.5 Cr), with chips accounting for only ₹45.0 Cr.
Because the two planning documents operate in parallel without reconciling chip ramp targets against the broader corporate model, investors and buyers must treat the ₹608 Cr figure as an SKU-level semiconductor ramp target and the ₹594.3 Cr figure as a distinct company-wide operational plan.

answers.q: Why do the business plan and the SKU Blueprint show different FY31 chip revenue?
answers.text:
Business Plan and SKU Blueprint Measure Different Portfolios and Timelines
The SKU Blueprint and the September 2026 financial model show sharply different FY31 chip revenue figures because they represent separate planning scopes and timelines: the Blueprint models dedicated semiconductor ramp revenue across eleven mature-node chips, while the financial model predates the Blueprint and allocates the vast majority of company turnover to non-chip systems.
Chip Ramp Focus vs Company-Wide Segmentation
In the SKU Blueprint (October 2026), FY31 revenue is projected at ₹608 Cr based solely on the approval schedules of eleven mature-node chips, with ₹1,000 Cr defined as a full run-rate stretch target rather than an FY31 expectation. The individual SKU lines sum to ₹609 Cr, with 71% carried by the BLDC motor controller and smart-meter SoC.
By contrast, the September 2026 financial model covers whole-company operations totaling ₹594.3 Cr in FY31, within which the Semiconductors segment contributes just ₹45.0 Cr. The balance of the model's revenue is dominated by the Systems division (₹501.9 Cr), alongside Robotics (₹28.9 Cr) and Sensors (₹18.5 Cr). Comparing chip revenue between the two documents reveals a 13.5-fold gap.
Unintegrated Modeling Cycles
This discrepancy persists because the earlier corporate financial model was published before the SKU Blueprint was finalized and has not yet integrated the detailed eleven-chip rollout schedule. Corporate planning indicates that a revised financial model (v4) incorporating the Blueprint's chip revenue trajectory will be published prior to Tranche 2 capital deployment.

Per-SKU Cost and Margin Breakdown
The SKU portfolio data calculates specific estimated gross margin ranges for four mature-node designs at representative selling prices: the Voltage supervisor models a 66–82% gross margin at a $0.50 price point (costing $0.09–0.17), while the Interface transceiver models a 68–82% gross margin at $0.95 (costing $0.17–0.30).
For the larger digital parts, the Motor controller (fan cut) estimates a 53–73% gross margin at $1.00 (costing $0.27–0.47), and the DG32-Max secure MCU estimates a 58–76% gross margin at $5.50 (costing $1.30–2.30). The portfolio documentation notes that all these figures remain assumptions until actual volume manufacturing quotes are secured.

answers.q: How long do automotive customers take to approve a new chip, according to the plan?
answers.text:
Automotive Chip Approvals Take 18 to 36 Months Under the Plan
According to the portfolio plan, automotive customers take 18 to 36 months to approve a new chip through the required AEC-Q100 qualification and carmaker design-in process before volume purchasing begins.
Approval Process and Timeline
The SKU Blueprint documents establish that entering the automotive sector requires passing AEC-Q100 standards alongside direct carmaker design-in cycles, taking an estimated 18 to 36 months before volume revenue can be realized.
Impact on Revenue Ramp

answers.q: What safety mechanism stops the inverter if the DG32-LITE CPU hangs?
answers.text:
Windowed Watchdog Detects Hangs While Complete Inverter Shutdown Path Remains Unspecified
In the DG32-LITE architecture, CPU hangs are detected by an integrated windowed watchdog within the safety core. However, the published documents do not detail the exact physical connection or signaling path from the watchdog timeout to the inverter gate driver.
Watchdog Hang Detection
The DG32-LITE safety core incorporates a windowed watchdog configured so that an update that arrives either too early or too late triggers a fault condition, specifically trapping software hangs as well as runaway execution. This watchdog arms only after firmware explicitly enables it, preventing boot deadlocks.
While datapath core mismatches explicitly assert the FAULT_N pin to turn off the inverter gate driver in hardware, the published architecture documentation does not describe whether the windowed watchdog directly asserts FAULT_N or relies on a watchdog reset signal to disable the power stage.
The published documentation does not specify the precise hardware routing connecting the windowed watchdog timeout signal to the inverter bridge shutoff or gate-driver enable path, nor does it confirm whether a watchdog timeout asserts FAULT_N or triggers a core reset.

answers.q: What is the development cost range for the planned chips?
answers.text:
Planned Chip Development Costs Total ₹41.7 Cr to ₹91.2 Cr Across Eleven SKUs
Across the entire planned portfolio of eleven chips, total development cost is projected at ₹41.7 Cr to ₹91.2 Cr, with individual chip costs spanning from ₹2.1 Cr to ₹12.8 Cr depending on design complexity and process node requirements.
Individual Chip Cost Ranges
At the individual product level, planned development costs vary widely based on specialized silicon processes and circuit requirements. The lowest-cost device is the SKU-10 DG32-Max Secure MCU at ₹2.1 Cr–₹4.3 Cr, while the highest-cost designs are the SKU-7 4D Radar RF at ₹6.4 Cr–₹12.8 Cr and the SKU-1 BLDC Motor Controller at ₹5.2 Cr–₹11.1 Cr.
Other planned SKUs fall within moderate expenditure bands. For example, the SKU-11 SOH-Aware BMS Controller is budgeted at ₹3.4 Cr to ₹7.8 Cr including qualification, while the SKU-8 Display Driver is budgeted at ₹2.4 Cr to ₹5.3 Cr.
Composition and Phasing of Development Expenditures
The development cost encompasses a prototype run followed by a production mask set and qualification for each target market. While prototype costs are based on quotes, production mask sets and qualification costs are planning estimates.
Annual planned development expenditures are phased across multiple fiscal years as chips are developed: ₹4–9 Cr in FY27, ₹13–27 Cr in FY28, ₹10–23 Cr in FY29, ₹8–18 Cr in FY30, and ₹6–14 Cr in FY31. The planned funding strategy utilizes staged tranches, where initial funding covers prototypes and subsequent capital funds production masks and qualification.

answers.q: What are the biggest unresolved risks DeepGrid discloses?
answers.text:
DeepGrid Identifies Timing Validation and Packaging Partnerships as Unresolved Risks
DeepGrid explicitly discloses that while several operational challenges have manageable remedies, two core technical and supply chain issues remain genuinely unresolved: proving its 200 MHz clock frequency target via published timing analysis and securing a named packaging and testing partner.
Unproven Core Clock Speed
The primary unproven technical claim is the operational clock frequency of the silicon. DeepGrid notes that its 200 MHz operating speed represents a design target rather than measured silicon performance, and static timing analyses have not yet been published against specific factory design kits.
Because the clock capability has only been demonstrated on FPGA prototypes up to 81.25 MHz, physical silicon performance remains unvalidated until per-chip timing runs are executed and published on the target manufacturing process.
Absence of Packaging and Assembly Infrastructure
On the operational side, DeepGrid acknowledges the complete absence of an established packaging supply chain. Multi-chip integrations require designated assembly partners, per-chip screening, and packaging test capabilities that are not yet contracted.
Commercial execution will likely remain constrained until external assembly agreements and testing lines are secured to convert fabricated wafers into commercial packaged units.

answers.q: What does SKU-10 do and what clock does it target?
answers.text:
SKU-10 Functions as a Secure Lockstep MCU Targeting 100 MHz
SKU-10 (DG32-Max Secure MCU) is designed as a secure general-purpose microcontroller with dual lockstep cores and integrated hardware security, targeting an operating clock frequency of 100 MHz.
Core Functions and Hardware Features
SKU-10 consolidates a general-purpose processor and a secure element onto a single die, replacing multi-chip implementations. It features two DGridRiscV processors operating in lockstep, built-in cryptographic instructions, a 4 KB instruction cache, 128 KB of error-corrected memory, and a boot ROM that verifies digital signatures within 309 ms from reset.
The microcontroller includes integrated peripherals such as CAN-FD, a 9-bit ADC, temperature and supply monitors, on-chip clocks, and debug access, exposing 44 signal pins in a 64-pin package. Because the SKY130 process lacks OTP or eFuse, device secrets and rollback counters are stored using a 1 kbit ReRAM macro, while root keys reside in mask ROM.
Clock Target and Applications
SKU-10 specifies a 100 MHz product target on the SKY130 node, which the architecture establishes as sufficient for handling its planned control and cryptographic workloads.
The part is planned for deployment across industrial controllers, drone flight controllers and ESCs, EV body and charger controllers, and IoT gateways, while also serving as an internal captive host platform for SKU-1 and SKU-11.

The published documentation does not report completion of design rule checking (DRC) or layout versus schematic (LVS) sign-off for SKU-1. Instead, the design is currently documented as having completed register-transfer level (RTL) design and analog schematic simulation, with physical fabrication scheduled for the first multi-project wafer (MPW) run.
SKU-1 Current Maturity is Limited to RTL and Schematics
According to the October 2026 SKU Blueprint, SKU-1's digital architecture is at the RTL stage, while its analog gate-drive and sensing paths are at schematic design and SPICE simulation status. Layout-level physical verification steps such as DRC and LVS are not mentioned as completed.
Because physical layout sign-offs like DRC and LVS occur after full physical place-and-route and custom layout assembly, the current status confirms that tape-out sign-off has not yet been achieved ahead of the planned cycle-1 shuttle.
The published documentation contains no records, reports, or timestamps confirming whether physical place-and-route, DRC, or LVS verification runs have been executed or closed for SKU-1.
